summary: MINERVA is an AI-powered fire safety intelligence platform that transforms NASA combustion research into clear, evidence-based insights. With customizable environments for Earth, Mars, and the Moon, users can explore fire behavior and compare two scenarios side by side to evaluate potential safety implications. By connecting scientific findings with practical engineering decisions, MINERVA helps pave the way for safer and more comfortable human space exploration.
details:
MINERVA turns NASA's microgravity combustion archive into a tool anyone can question: you describe a fire scenario for a spacecraft cabin, a Moon or Mars habitat, and it answers with the closest real test runs, a labelled physics approximation of how fast the flame would spread, and an honest statement of how well the data covers what you asked. It was built for the NASA Space Apps microgravity combustion challenge, and it runs entirely in the browser from 1,887 test runs drawn from 17 NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) investigations.

The guiding idea is that fire in space is not a smaller version of fire on Earth. Without buoyancy, a flame has no upward plume, so it spreads differently, survives at oxygen levels that would not sustain it on the ground, and is harder for a crew to recognise. The data describing that behaviour already exists in NASA's published experiment tables, but it exists as spreadsheets of raw columns, one per investigation, with different units, different naming conventions and no shared interface. MINERVA is the layer that makes those tables answer a question a human would actually ask.

What it does and how it works

The user builds a scenario and MINERVA answers it from data first and physics second, keeping the two labelled apart at every step. In the scenario builder the user chooses a fuel type (solid material, liquid droplet or gas jet), a gravity preset (microgravity at about 10⁻⁶ g, lunar 0.17 g, Martian 0.38 g or Earth 1 g), a specific fuel or material drawn from the dataset with its run count shown, an oxygen concentration, an airflow speed, a chamber pressure in kPa and a flow direction (concurrent, opposed or quiescent). A habitat row lets the same choice be made by picking a destination rather than a number, which sets the gravity preset behind the scenes. Pressing Analyze scenario then runs four stages.

The first stage is the nearest-run search. Within the chosen fuel type, every test run in the dataset is given a distance from the user's scenario: the root-mean-square of the differences in oxygen, log pressure, airflow and flow direction, with each difference divided by that variable's standard deviation across the data so that no variable dominates merely because its units are large, plus a penalty when the run used a different fuel. A variable a run never recorded is counted as one standard deviation away rather than silently treated as a match, and a variable that no run of that fuel recorded at all is dropped from the calculation instead of distorting it. The ten nearest runs then drive the outcome summary, and confidence is reported from data density, namely how many runs fall within half a standard deviation of the scenario.

The second stage is the physics approximation of flame spread. Because many NASA runs record their test conditions but never recorded an outcome, a data-only answer would often be silent. MINERVA therefore derives an order-of-magnitude spread rate from de Ris thermal flame-spread scaling. It starts from the published limiting oxygen index of the material (about 17.3% for PMMA, 25% for silicone, 47% for Ultem, 19% for SIBAL and 28% for Nomex), then shifts that limit for the scenario: raising it by about five points when total flow is near zero and oxygen can only arrive by diffusion, lowering it in reduced gravity where gentle flow lets some materials burn below their Earth limit, and raising it slightly as pressure falls. Spread rate is then scaled from the margin above that shifted limit, quadratically for thermally thick fuels and linearly for thin ones, with corrections for buoyant flow (roughly 30 cm/s × √g), forced airflow and blow-off under strong opposed flow. Droplets are rated instead by their burning-rate constant K, since a droplet fire has no surface to spread across, and gas jets are given no spread estimate at all because the concept does not apply to them.

The third stage is the hazard verdict, which deliberately prefers measurement over modelling. It reads recorded outcomes first, such as CFI-G ignition results, FLEX extinction events and Saffire burn observations, and falls back to the physics approximation only where no outcome was recorded. The fourth stage is the explanation. Every statement in the results view is tagged either DATA or PHYSICS so the reader always knows whether they are being told what NASA measured or what a model estimated, and the spread estimate is printed alongside any rate the nearest runs actually measured, so the approximation is checked against reality on screen. On the published claude.ai page the interpretation is written by Claude from the same evidence; opened locally or on GitHub Pages, the page falls back to a rule-based interpretation so the tool never depends on a network call to be useful.

Around these four stages sit the supporting views: a coverage chart showing where the scenario sits relative to the tested ranges, the five most relevant runs with their source file and row, a list of every investigation in the dataset with ranges computed from its own runs, and a Compare scenarios view with an editable scenario B so two habitats can be set side by side and the shift in both the nearest runs and the physics estimate can be read directly.

Benefits

The first benefit is accessibility of data that already exists but is effectively unreadable. NASA's PSI tables are public, but using them means opening sixteen separate CSV files, reconciling pressures given in bar, mmHg and atmospheres, recognising that one table's oxygen column refers to a burner jet rather than the chamber atmosphere, and knowing which rows are real test runs rather than test-design ranges or day summaries. MINERVA absorbs all of that once, in a documented build step, so a student or a mission planner spends their attention on the question instead of on data cleaning.

The second is honest uncertainty. Every result carries its provenance: the DATA and PHYSICS tags, the confidence figure derived from how many runs genuinely sit near the scenario, the explicit warning that every run in the dataset was performed in microgravity so Moon, Mars and Earth readouts are extrapolations, and the named source file and row behind each cited study. A tool that answered every scenario with equal confidence would be more satisfying and far less trustworthy; MINERVA is built so that a thin region of the data looks thin on screen.

The third is speed of comparison. The compare view and the habitat row turn what would otherwise be a research task into a few seconds of interaction, which is what makes the tool useful for teaching. A student can hold a material fixed and watch the estimated spread rate and the nearest runs change as oxygen rises from 21% to 34%, or as gravity drops from Earth to lunar, and the counterintuitive result, that lower gravity with gentle airflow can let a material burn below its Earth oxygen limit, becomes something they discover rather than something they are told.

Intended impact

The project's name points at its purpose: a safe space journey for all. As crewed missions move from a single station in low Earth orbit toward lunar surface habitats and eventually Mars transits, fire safety stops being a solved problem. Exploration atmospheres under consideration, such as 56.5 kPa at 34% oxygen, sit outside the conditions most Earth-based flammability certification assumes, and partial gravity has never been tested in the PSI combustion archive at all. MINERVA is intended to make that gap visible rather than paper over it, and to put the question of what happens to a flame in an unfamiliar atmosphere in front of the people who will have to answer it.

For students and the public, the aim is conceptual: to replace the intuition that fire always rises with an understanding of why it does so on Earth and what happens when buoyancy is removed. The landing section states the idea plainly, that without gravity a flame loses its direction but not its danger, and the rest of the interface exists to let someone test that claim against real measurements instead of accepting it on authority.

For mission planners, educators and early-stage researchers, the aim is practical triage. MINERVA does not replace certified material flammability testing and says so prominently; what it does is let someone narrow a question before committing to expensive work, by showing which NASA investigations already touch a given region of the parameter space, which materials have been characterised there, and where no run exists at all. A scenario that returns low confidence and no nearby runs is itself a useful result, because it identifies a region of the design space where no evidence yet exists.

More broadly, the project is meant to demonstrate a pattern for open scientific data. NASA's PSI archive is one of many public datasets whose value is limited less by access than by usability. MINERVA's build script, which documents every cleaning decision and preserves every original row verbatim, is intended as a reusable argument that making such data explorable is a legitimate contribution in its own right.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The stack was chosen for longevity and zero friction rather than for novelty. There is no framework, no bundler and no package manager in the delivered site, which means the project has no dependency that can break it and will still open in a browser years from now.

Layer

Choice

Why

Markup

A single index.html, about 320 lines, holding three views (builder, results, about)

One file keeps routing and state trivial and makes the whole site inspectable

Styling

Hand-written CSS, about 270 lines, no framework

Full control of the space-themed visual language at a fraction of a framework's weight

Application logic

Vanilla JavaScript, about 670 lines, zero imports

Matching, outcome summaries, the physics approximation, charting, routing and the flame animation, with no dependency to install or audit

Animation

HTML5 Canvas 2D with requestAnimationFrame and ResizeObserver

A particle flame that responds to gravity, oxygen and airflow, drawn without any graphics library

Data pipeline

Python 3 using only the standard library (csv, json, re, statistics, collections, pathlib)

Reproducible cleaning with no third-party install step

Delivered data

A generated data/psi_data.js loaded as a plain script

Avoids fetch, so the site works from the local filesystem with no server

Typography

Chakra Petch, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono via Google Fonts

A technical, instrument-panel feel, with a graceful fallback to system fonts offline

AI layer

Claude, called through the host page's sampling capability when published on claude.ai

Writes the scenario interpretation from the same evidence the rule-based path uses, and is strictly optional

Version control

Git and GitHub, with per-member branches (main, akbar-branch, aura-branch) merged into main

Parallel work on data, interface and logic without blocking each other

Hosting

Static hosting; GitHub Pages or a local file

No server, database or API key required to run

The hardware story is deliberately minimal and this is a design position rather than a limitation. MINERVA requires no sensors, microcontrollers or custom hardware: it runs on any laptop, tablet or phone with a modern browser, and the real hardware behind it is NASA's, namely the Combustion Integrated Rack and the Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station, together with the Saffire experiments flown aboard Cygnus resupply vehicles, which produced the runs the tool reads.

The dataset itself comes from NASA's Physical Science Informatics repository, covering seventeen investigations: BASS and BASS-II, Saffire I, II and III, FLEX and FLEX-2, SAME and SAME-R, CFI, CFI-G, SPICE, ACME Flame Design, ACME BRE and ACME CLD Flame, including both normal and inverse flame tables where they exist. The merged file holds 1,929 rows, of which 1,887 are used for matching after 42 exact duplicates are dropped.

How the project is creative

The central creative move is treating a spreadsheet archive as a search space rather than a reference. The obvious thing to build from NASA's PSI tables is a browser: filters, a sortable grid, a download button. MINERVA inverts the interaction. The user never queries the data; they describe a situation, and the tool finds the data. That reframing is what makes the archive usable by someone who does not already know what FLEX or SIBAL means, and it is the difference between publishing data and answering a question.

Second, the project fuses two kinds of evidence that are usually kept in separate tools, and does so without blurring them. Experimental data and analytical scaling theory normally live in different papers and different software; here a nearest-neighbour search over real runs and a de Ris scaling estimate appear in the same readout, each labelled, with the estimate printed next to any spread rate the nearby runs actually measured so that the model is visibly audited by the data. Choosing to display that comparison, including when the two disagree, is a deliberate design decision in favour of the reader's judgement over the tool's authority.

Third, the statistical scaling of the distance metric is a quiet piece of creative engineering. Dividing each variable's difference by its own standard deviation in the dataset means the search is not biased by units, so a pressure difference measured in hundreds of kilopascals cannot drown out an oxygen difference measured in single percentage points. Counting a missing value as one standard deviation away, rather than as zero or as a match, means an incomplete run is penalised in proportion to its incompleteness instead of being silently promoted or discarded. These are small decisions that determine whether the results are trustworthy.

Fourth, the visual and narrative design carries the science. The canvas flame is driven by the same scenario parameters as the analysis, so when gravity falls the plume loses its upward stretch and becomes the spherical diffusion flame that microgravity actually produces: the animation teaches the central concept rather than decorating it. The habitat row, the five-stage journey and the framing sentence that in space fire has no up give a dataset of combustion runs a narrative shape, which is what allows a technical tool to be approached by a general audience without diluting what it reports.

Fifth, the project is creative in what it refuses to claim. The limits are stated in the interface, not buried: many runs record conditions but no outcome, spread rates are order-of-magnitude approximations, the flame is illustrative, every run is microgravity so all partial-gravity readouts are extrapolations, and nothing here substitutes for certified flammability testing. Building the caveats into the product rather than the footnotes is an unusual choice for a competition entry and, we would argue, the correct one for a safety tool.

Factors the team considered

Scientific integrity of the source data. The largest share of the work went into the data pipeline rather than the interface, because the source tables disagree with each other in ways that would silently corrupt any analysis. Pressures arrive in bar, mmHg and atmospheres and are converted to a single unit. The inverse-flame tables of ACME Flame Design and CFI-G report oxygen fraction in the burner jet, up to 85%, rather than in the chamber atmosphere, so those rows are flagged with an explicit o2_location column and excluded from ambient-oxygen comparison. Formatting artefacts were caught and corrected with the original value preserved: ACME BRE's "3400%" and "2100%" read correctly as 34 and 21, and CLD Flame's fuel labels CH5 through CH14 proved to be a spreadsheet fill-down artefact for CH₄. Eight negative airflow values in SPICE were left in place and flagged rather than quietly deleted. Non-test rows were excluded from matching rather than from the dataset: smoke experiments, test-design range rows, day summaries, inverse flames and a cleaning run are all still visible, just not treated as comparable test runs. Every row retains its untouched source values in a raw_row_json field alongside its source file and row number, so any transformation can be audited or reversed.

Stating assumptions instead of hiding them. Where a value had to be assumed, the assumption is stored with the run and shown in the interface. SPICE's oxygen is set to 20.9% because its co-flow is air; samples described only by shape, such as a rod, sphere or film, are kept and labelled "material not stated" rather than guessed at; SAME-R's year was taken from the investigation description because the source dates omit it; and Saffire and BASS-II atmosphere types are marked as inferred, with the basis recorded.

Honesty about the gravity gap. The most consequential constraint is that every run in the PSI combustion archive was performed in microgravity. There is no partial-gravity combustion data for Moon or Mars conditions. The team's decision was neither to hide the gap nor to abandon those habitats, but to let the user ask the question and label the answer as extrapolated every time, with the habitat cards stating plainly that Moon, Mars and Earth have zero runs in the dataset.

Accessibility and inclusion. The name is "Safe Space Journey for All" and the interface tries to earn the last two words. Semantic landmarks, aria-label and aria-current attributes and aria-pressed state on the habitat controls make the tool navigable by screen reader; decorative elements including the starfield and the flame canvas are marked aria-hidden so they are not announced. The animation respects the operating system's prefers-reduced-motion setting. Content is usable on a phone, and the habitat row is swipeable with arrow controls for anyone who cannot swipe.

Offline and low-resource use. The decision to load data as a plain script rather than via fetch was made specifically so the site works when opened directly from a filesystem, with no server and no internet connection. This matters for classrooms and regions where reliable connectivity cannot be assumed, and it is why the AI interpretation is an enhancement with a rule-based fallback rather than a requirement.

Scope discipline. The team considered running a numerical combustion simulation and decided against it. A CFD model would have been more impressive and less honest: it would have produced confident-looking output from assumptions the team could not validate within the project's scope. Choosing a labelled order-of-magnitude approximation checked against real measurements, and saying clearly that it is an approximation, was judged the more defensible engineering decision.

Collaboration under time pressure. Work was split across Git branches so that the data pipeline, the interface and the analysis logic could progress in parallel, then merged into main. The dataset was built in two documented versions, a nine-investigation core and a seventeen-investigation expansion, so that the site always had working data to develop against while coverage was still growing.
